cards.title: Write copy for 20–35% of visitors, not all of them
cards.summary: Copy Hackers' core rule: target a specific qualified segment of roughly 20–35% of your audience instead of neutralizing copy to appeal to everyone.
cards.use_when: Deciding who a product page, landing page or ad should speak to before writing any copy — especially when a stakeholder asks for messaging that 'works for everyone'.
steps: Define the specific segment you are writing for — the people most likely to buy, not the total addressable market. The source's guidance is to aim copy at roughly 20–35% of your visitors rather than 100%.
Accept that generic messaging written to avoid offending anyone produces copy no one feels is for them; narrow targeting is a deliberate trade, not an oversight.
Pull the segment's own words from customer interviews, surveys and forums (see the research card) so the narrowing is based on real language rather than a demographic guess.
Check that the chosen segment is financially viable: the segment must be large enough that 20–35% of actual traffic can support the offer.
Apply the same segment definition consistently across hero copy, subheads and CTAs so the page reads as one conversation with one person.
caveats: 20–35% is a source-specific heuristic for how narrowly to target, not a calculated benchmark; adjust to your traffic and margin.
Very small or early-stage stores may not have enough traffic to sub-segment this tightly — verify before splitting.

cards.title: Build a product positioning matrix before writing copy
cards.summary: Document an exhaustive matrix mapping every product feature to customer pain points, unique advantages, concrete benefits and priority rankings.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write or rewrite PDP, landing page or ad copy and needing a single source of truth for what each feature actually does for the customer.
steps: List every product feature, including ones you consider minor — the source calls for an exhaustive matrix, not a highlight reel.
For each feature, record the customer pain point it addresses, in the customer's own terms, not internal product language.
Record the unique advantage: what this feature does that competitors' equivalent feature does not.
Write the concrete benefit — the outcome the customer gets — and rank features by priority so the most persuasive ones lead the page.
Use the completed matrix as the source document when drafting headlines, bullets and ad angles, so no copy claim appears that isn't traceable to a mapped benefit.
Refresh the matrix when the product, pricing or competitive set changes; treat it as a living document, not a one-off.
caveats: The matrix is only as good as the customer input behind the pain points; pairing it with interviews and review mining is what keeps it from being internal guesswork.

cards.title: Mine customer language instead of wordsmithing
cards.summary: Extract messaging directly from customer interviews, surveys, forums, exact search keywords and review phrases to eliminate guesswork and 'wordsmithing'.
cards.use_when: Starting messaging work for a new product, ad angle or PDP and needing the raw vocabulary and motivations customers actually use.
steps: Gather direct customer intelligence through interviews, surveys and forums before writing a single word of copy.
Search your own reviews, support tickets and the competitor reviews you can access, and collect the exact phrases customers use for the problem and the outcome.
Pull the exact search keywords customers use to find products like yours; keyword language often differs from internal product language.
Sort the collected phrases into pain points, motivations and objections, keeping the customer's wording intact rather than paraphrasing into brand-speak.
Draft headlines, bullets and ad hooks using those collected phrases so the copy sounds like the customer talking rather than a marketer polishing sentences.
Re-run this collection periodically — customer language shifts as the market matures.
caveats: Exact keywords and review phrases are inputs to phrasing, not a substitute for a positioning decision; you still choose which segment and benefit to lead with.

cards.title: Audit competitor content to map their value propositions and CTAs
cards.summary: Run a competitor content audit covering organic search and paid results to map value propositions, top-performing messages and calls to action.
cards.use_when: Positioning a new product, choosing an ad angle, or checking whether your current messaging has drifted into sameness with the category.
steps: Identify the direct competitors your target segment would actually compare you against, not every brand in the category.
For each, collect the content ranking in organic search for your core terms and the ads appearing for those terms in paid results.
For each asset, record the stated value proposition, the primary message, the call to action, and the angle or mechanism they lead with.
Compare across competitors to surface which messages repeat (likely category table stakes) and which are differentiated or underused.
Use the audit to choose where you will match table stakes and where you will lead with a different angle or unique mechanism.
Re-audit on a schedule, since competitors' messaging and paid creative rotate frequently.
caveats: The audit reveals what competitors claim, not what converts for them; treat it as an input to positioning, not proof of a winning message.
Ad platforms' interfaces and ad libraries change — verify the current tool for viewing competitor ads before relying on a specific method.

cards.title: Organize messages into a hierarchy the page can follow
cards.summary: After building the feature-benefit matrix, organize messages into a clear hierarchy so each page or ad leads with the highest-priority claim.
cards.use_when: Turning a positioning document into the actual order of arguments on a PDP, landing page or paid ad, when everything feels equally important.
steps: Take the ranked feature-benefit matrix and mark the single highest-priority benefit for the target segment — this becomes the hero message.
Place secondary benefits in descending priority as supporting sections, bullets or ad body copy.
Decide where objection-handling and proof belong in the sequence, typically after the primary claim and before the call to action.
Check that each level of the hierarchy speaks to the same segment so the page doesn't drift back toward generic messaging as it scrolls.
Use the same hierarchy across channels — PDP, landing page, paid creative — so a visitor arriving from an ad sees the claim they clicked on.
Test one hero-message variation at a time when validating the hierarchy rather than swapping the whole order.
caveats: The hierarchy is a positioning decision, not a conversion guarantee; validating which lead message performs best requires its own testing discipline.

input.text:
10-MCR / paid social creative and content

Goes here. Paid social creative production, hook writing, direct response video frameworks, creator/UGC scripting, static ad design, messaging strategies, evaluating stages of awareness, identifying new ad formats/angles, advertorials, unique mechanisms, and creative strategist workflows.

Not here.

Paid advertising performance metrics, ROAS, scaling rules, bidding, or ad-platform specific attribution -> 11-ADC

Conversion rate optimization (CRO) on core website pages or general analytics -> 06-MEA

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details professional copywriting and messaging strategy frameworks (customer research, feature-benefit matrices, competitor content audits, and target-segment messaging) focused on aligning web copy with actual customer language and motivations. modules: [MCR] topics: [creative strategy, messaging and positioning] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. creative strategy / Developing rigorous pre-writing messaging strategies and research frameworks. Gathering direct customer intelligence through interviews, surveys, and forums to uncover core customer pain points, motivations, and natural vocabulary before writing a single word. Conducting competitor content audits to map value propositions, top-performing messages, and calls to action across organic search and PPC results. messaging and positioning / Structuring copy around a specific, highly qualified target segment (targeting 20-35% of visitors rather than trying to appeal to 100% of the audience with generic messaging). Documenting exhaustive feature-benefit matrices and organizing messages into a clear messaging hierarchy. Leveraging customer and competitor language (such as exact search keywords and review phrases) to eliminate "wordsmithing" and craft compelling value propositions.

Look for. The core copywriting rule regarding audience targeting: writing for a specific, qualified market segment (20-35% of visitors) rather than neutralizing copy for the masses. The definition of a product positioning document: an exhaustive matrix mapping every product feature directly to customer pain points, unique advantages, concrete benefits, and priority rankings. The principle of customer-driven messaging: extracting messaging from customer language, keyword research, and competitor audits rather than internal assumptions.

Skip. General ebook publishing backgrounds, author biographies, or table of contents directories.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.
